newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian left offers plan to avert oil price hike.
newsitem.headline: Indian left offers plan to avert oil price hike.

text.p: An Indian communist party on Monday unveiled a strategy to stave off a looming oil price hike which the government of Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral is to decide later this week.

The plan, proposed by an ally of Gujral's 15-party United front coalition, calls for the government to return to the state-run oil sector surplus funds that have been diverted from it by earlier governments, and the elimination of customs and excise duties.

"The government is in fact squeezing the oil sector of its surplus to meet the overall fiscal deficit while the people are being continuously burdened with price hikes," Sitaram Yechury, a leader of the Communist Party of India (Marxist), said.

Analysts say the long-delayed oil price hike is necessary if the federal government is to bridge the oil pool deficit -- the money the government owes oil firms for selling petroleum products well below international rates.
The oil pool deficit was estimated at 155 billion rupees ($4.33 billion) at the end of March, the government said.
Gujral's government will meet on Sunday to discuss the price hike, after two earlier meetings ended inconclusively.
Yechury, writing in the Economic Times daily, said successive federal governments had "siphoned off" an 89-billion-rupee oil pool surplus during the years from 1989 onwards to help balance the books.
"This has been periodically siphoned off to meet the overall fiscal deficit," Yechury said.
"If this outstanding is returned at the government's interdepartmental interest rates, it would amount to 278.5 billion rupees as of March 31, 1997."
Yechury has also called for the removal of customs and excise duties levied on the oil sector, and estimated in the 1997/98 national budget to amount to over 196 billion rupees.
"It is the customs and excise duties that make these products so expensive here," he said.

The third prong of the left's long-term strategy calls for the government to pay to the oil sector a tax it has collected from oil companies for the development of indigenous production. The total sum so far collected amounts to 278 billion rupees.
"If the oil sector is not treated as the milch cow to meet revenue collection targets then the current oil pool deficit just does not exist," Yechury said.

In addition to these steps, action the government could take in the short-term included the rationalisation of natural gas prices, a tax on cars with 1,000 cc. engines and over, and cuts in customs duty on crude and diesel imports, Yechury said.

"The choice therefore is one of undertaking a series of measures that will spare the burdens on the working people and protect their livelihood rather than taking the shortcut of imposing an across-the-board price hike," Yechury said. ($1.00 = 35.78 rupees)
